newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-B.Philp says sees some improvement.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-B.Philp says sees some improvement.

text.p: Food ingredients group Burns Philp and Co has seen some improvement in its markets in the first two months of the year, managing director Ian Clack said.

"In most markets we are seeing some improvement in the first two months of the year," Clack said after the announcement of annual results. He also said the company may sell down further its stake in Applied Microbiology Inc of the U.S..
"We may sell it down further," Clack said.
Burns Philp has sold down its stake in AMBI to 49 percent from 63 percent over the past few years.
Clack said the 49 percent stake in Applied Microbiology was worth about US$40 million to US$45 million and it may be sold down further in the current year.
He said Burns Philp was also looking at divesting other non-core assets, but he would not specify which assets were being considered or when they might be sold.
Earlier, Burns Philp reported a A$61.8 million net loss for the year to June 30, 1996 after an abnormal loss after tax of A$136.6 million. It did not declare a dividend.
The abnormal loss was due largely to the recognition of the rationalisation of manufacturing and distribution facilities in North America.
Burns Philp's operating profit before abnormal items and tax fell to A$102.9 million from A$130.2 million the previous year.
It said the major factors contributing to the trading profit for the current year were the strong performance in the yeast and bakery businesses in North America and Europe.

"These gains were more than offset by the impact of higher costs of amortising the multi-year slotting contracts entered into in 1994/95 by the consumer businesses, increased raw material and packaging costs, competition and lower demand in our Australian businesses, competitive activity in the German spice market and the costs of expansion in Asia," it said.
Burns Philp paid U.S. supermarkets during a price war in 1994/95 to put their products on certain more attractive shelves. These contracts are known as slotting contracts.
